title: U.S. House · Pennsylvania's 8th Congressional District
area: Northeastern Pennsylvania, including Luzerne, Lackawanna (Scranton, Wilkes-Barre), Wayne, Pike, and Monroe counties.

context.text: Ballotpedia identified this race as a battleground. Rob Bresnahan Jr. defeated then-incumbent Rep. Matt Cartwright (D) 50.7%-49.1% in 2024, and Donald Trump (R) carried the district 53.8%-45.4% over Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee named Cognetti to its "Red to Blue" program and the National Republican Congressional Committee named Bresnahan to its "Patriot" program.
Paige Cognetti was unopposed in the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary after Eric Stone did not make the ballot; Rob Bresnahan was unopposed in the Republican primary.

According to The Cook Political Report's Erin Covey, Democrats have focused on Bresnahan's history of stock trading in the House after he said he supported a ban on members doing so; between January 2025 and February 2026 he executed 650 trades. A representative for Bresnahan said he "has never traded his own stocks and an outside financial institution manages his investments." Republicans have focused on Cognetti's record as Scranton mayor, including a Politico report that she "helped secure a state grant for a new Fidelity Bank headquarters, where her husband's uncle sits on the board."

summary.text: Rob Bresnahan Jr. is the Republican incumbent U.S. Representative for Pennsylvania's 8th District, elected in 2024 after defeating then-incumbent Matt Cartwright. Before Congress he was chief executive officer of his family's electrical contracting company, Kuharchik Construction, and founded a real estate development group. He serves on the Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture and Small Business committees.

background.text: Born in 1990 in Kingston, Pennsylvania, and raised in the Wyoming Valley, where, according to his official biography, he helped in his family's electrical contracting business as a child.
Earned a B.S. in business administration from the University of Scranton in 2012.

Became chief executive officer of Kuharchik Construction, a commercial electrical contractor, in 2013; according to his official biography the company grew to more than 150 employees under his leadership.
Founded a real estate development group focused on renovating and repurposing buildings, and was owner of RPB Ventures, a real estate development company.
Was named one of the Northeastern Pennsylvania Business Journal's 20 Under 40 in 2018, according to his official biography.

Before Congress, served as chairman of a Joint Apprentice Training Committee, as a trustee of IBEW Local 163 benefit funds, and as treasurer of the nonprofit tecBridge; he was also president of the Luzerne County SPCA and sat on boards including Junior Achievement, Big Brothers Big Sisters of Northeastern Pennsylvania and the Luzerne County Industrial Development Authority.
Won his first election in November 2024, defeating incumbent Democrat Matt Cartwright 50.7% to 49.1%.
Serves on the Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture and Small Business committees, and is vice chair of the Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

Is a member of caucuses including the Problem Solvers Caucus and the Congressional Apprenticeship Caucus; lives in Northeastern Pennsylvania with his wife, Chelsea, and is a licensed helicopter pilot, according to his official biography.

priorities.text: Campaign website says that during his tenure he "focused on cutting red tape, defending working families, and delivering results for his hometown region," citing his work on the Transportation and Infrastructure, Small Business, and Agriculture committees.
priorities.quote: focused on cutting red tape, defending working families, and delivering results for his hometown region

priorities.text: Campaigned in 2024 on banning members of Congress from trading individual stocks and introduced a House bill in May 2025 that would have forbidden the practice.

record.text: Assigned to the Committee on Agriculture, the Committee on Small Business, and the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure in the 2025-2026 Congress.

Introduced a House bill in May 2025 that would ban members of Congress from trading individual stocks, after campaigning on such a ban; a Philadelphia Inquirer analysis found he made 617 trades totaling $7.24 million in 2025. His office said the trades are handled by an outside financial adviser and that he has never traded his own stocks.
Elected to the U.S. House in 2024, defeating incumbent Matt Cartwright 50.7% to 49.1%.

candidates.name: Paige Cognetti

summary.text: Paige Cognetti is the Democratic nominee for Pennsylvania's 8th District and the Mayor of Scranton. She grew up in Beaverton, Oregon, worked in the Obama administration and as an investment advisor, and moved to Scranton in 2016. She served on the Scranton School Board before being elected mayor in a 2019 special election, running as an independent, and took office in January 2020. She launched her congressional campaign in September 2025 and is running on an anti-corruption agenda that includes a ban on congressional stock trading.

background.text: Graduated summa cum laude from the University of Oregon's Clark Honors College with a B.A. in English literature, and holds an M.B.A. from Harvard Business School.

Worked as a fundraiser and project director on political campaigns, including Barack Obama's 2008 presidential campaign, and then served in the Obama administration as a senior advisor to the Under Secretary for International Affairs at the U.S. Treasury Department.
Worked as an investment advisor in New York City, including briefly at Goldman Sachs, before moving to Scranton in 2016.
Served on the Scranton School Board from 2017 to 2018.
Advised the Pennsylvania Auditor General on oversight of public school districts and care for older adults.

Ran for mayor of Scranton as an independent under the slogan "Paige Against the Machine" in a 2019 special election and became the first woman to hold the office. Former mayor Bill Courtright later pleaded guilty, on July 2, 2020, to conspiracy, bribery and extortion and was sentenced to seven years in prison.
Sworn in as mayor on January 6, 2020, and won re-election to a full term in November 2021.

Says that as mayor she turned down the city car and a pay raise and balanced the budget, ending a 30-year period of financial distress for the city; she lives in Scranton with her husband and two daughters.

priorities.text: Launched her campaign attacking incumbent Rob Bresnahan's record of stock trading in Congress after he campaigned on banning it, saying he made 600 trades in a single year.
priorities.quote: Rob ran for Congress on a promise to ban stock trades. This year, he's already made 600 trades — 600. I'm running for Congress because people here deserve a lot better than a rich kid disrespecting our hard work and proud legacy.

priorities.text: Her campaign launch ad accused Bresnahan of "ripping Medicaid away from Pennsylvania families" by voting for the budget reconciliation bill known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and criticized the timing of some of his stock trades relative to policy events.
priorities.quote: Sold Chinese stocks the week of a tariff. Buys missile stocks before a war, buys jet stocks before a big contract.

positions.summary: Campaign launch ad accused incumbent Bresnahan of cutting Medicaid coverage for Pennsylvania families by voting for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, implying opposition to those cuts.
positions.quote: ripping Medicaid away from Pennsylvania families by voting for President Donald Trump's budget bill

candidates.researchNotes: Her personal campaign website could not be reached (the domain names most associated with her name redirect to a National Republican Congressional Committee attack site); positions are drawn from her campaign launch video and news coverage. As Scranton mayor she has official actions on record, but a full account of her mayoral record was outside this basic-tier research budget.

Sources differ on whether Cognetti was elected mayor in 2019 or 2020; the guide uses the 2019 special election and the January 6, 2020 swearing-in reported by Ballotpedia and the City of Scranton.
